title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

standard_text: Physical and chemical changes in daily life; signs of a chemical change; reversible and irreversible changes; crystallisation; rusting; desirable and undesirable, slow and fast changes (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 5).
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 7 Science worksheets for NCERT Curiosity Chapter 5: physical and chemical changes, signs of a chemical change, reversible and irreversible changes, crystallisation, rusting and the reaction of vinegar with baking soda. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A chemical change makes a new substance.
key_sub: A physical change alters only shape, size or state.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a physical change, only properties such as shape, size or state change and no new substance forms: ice melts, paper is torn, sugar dissolves. In a chemical change, a new substance forms, often with a gas, heat, light, a colour change or a smell: paper burns, iron rusts, milk curdles.

Vinegar and baking soda give carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky. Pure crystals can be got from a solution by crystallisation. Some changes are desirable (cooking), some undesirable (rusting); some are slow, some fast.

Example

Is cooking an egg physical or chemical?

it cannot become a raw egg again

new substances form

Answer: chemical

Example

CO₂ through lime water?

calcium carbonate forms

Answer: it turns milky

Common mistakes

  • Calling every reversible change chemical.
  • Thinking dissolving is a chemical change.
  • Forgetting that burning a candle shows both changes.

faq.q: How can you tell a chemical change?
faq.a: A new substance forms, often shown by a gas, heat or light, a colour change or a new smell.

faq.q: Why is the melting of wax physical but its burning chemical?
faq.a: Melted wax can become solid again; burning makes new substances such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.
